claim: The retina consumes massive amounts of energy.
source: The retina consumes massive amounts of energy, yet its metabolism and substrate exploitation remain poorly understood.
evidence: Supported by citations to Country, 2017 and Wong-Riley, 2010 in the introduction section.

claim: The mammalian retina is thought to strongly rely on energy-inefficient glycolysis, even though oxygen is available and high-yield oxidative phosphorylation is possible.
source: Paradoxically, the mammalian retina is thought to strongly rely on energy-inefficient glycolysis, even though oxygen is available and high-yield oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) possible (Swarup et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Swarup et al., 2019.

claim: Aerobic glycolysis in the retina releases large amounts of lactate, as reported in the 1920s by Warburg.
source: This aerobic glycolysis releases large amounts of lactate, as already reported in the 1920s by Warburg, 1925.
evidence: Supported by citation to Warburg, 1925.

claim: High retinal energy demand is linked to the extraordinary single-photon sensitivity of photoreceptors.
source: High retinal energy demand is linked to the extraordinary single-photon sensitivity of photoreceptors (Wong-Riley, 2010; Okawa et al., 2008; Ames, 1992), and to lipid synthesis for the constant renewal of photoreceptor outer segments (Chinchore et al., 2017; Young, 1967).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wong-Riley, 2010; Okawa et al., 2008; Ames, 1992.

claim: High retinal energy demand is linked to lipid synthesis for the constant renewal of photoreceptor outer segments.
source: High retinal energy demand is linked to the extraordinary single-photon sensitivity of photoreceptors (Wong-Riley, 2010; Okawa et al., 2008; Ames, 1992), and to lipid synthesis for the constant renewal of photoreceptor outer segments (Chinchore et al., 2017; Young, 1967).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chinchore et al., 2017; Young, 1967.

claim: Cones spend around twice as much energy as rods.
source: Cones spend around twice as much energy as rods (Ingram et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ingram et al., 2020.

claim: Photoreceptors are not connected to the vasculature and are nourished by other retinal cell types, including retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells or Müller glial cells (MGCs).
source: Photoreceptors are not connected to the vasculature and are nourished by other retinal cell types, including retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) (Strauss, 2005) cells or Müller glial cells (MGCs).
evidence: Supported by citation to Strauss, 2005.

claim: Photoreceptors can experience changes in energy demand on a millisecond timescale, from very high in the dark, to 4–10 times lower in light.
source: Moreover, photoreceptors can experience changes in energy demand on a millisecond timescale, from very high in the dark, to 4–10 times lower in light (Okawa et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Okawa et al., 2008.

claim: Glycolysis provides for rapid but inefficient adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production.
source: Glycolysis provides for rapid but inefficient adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production, while Krebs-cycle and OXPHOS are very efficient but much slower.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about glycolysis.

claim: Krebs-cycle and OXPHOS are very efficient but much slower than glycolysis.
source: Glycolysis provides for rapid but inefficient adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production, while Krebs-cycle and OXPHOS are very efficient but much slower.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about oxidative phosphorylation.

claim: A recent hypothesis proposed that photoreceptors use predominantly aerobic glycolysis, with the resultant lactate utilised by the RPE and MGCs for OXPHOS.
source: A recent hypothesis proposed that photoreceptors use predominantly aerobic glycolysis, with the resultant lactate utilised by the RPE and MGCs for OXPHOS (Kanow et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kanow et al., 2017.

claim: The high density of mitochondria in photoreceptor inner segments strongly suggests an extensive use of OXPHOS.
source: However, this concept contrasts with the high density of mitochondria in photoreceptor inner segments, which strongly suggest an extensive use of OXPHOS.
evidence: Based on inference from structural observations.

claim: The Cahill-cycle involves pyruvate being transaminated using glutamate to yield alanine and α-ketoglutarate.
source: Alternative pathways for ATP generation include the Cahill-cycle, where pyruvate is transaminated using, for instance, glutamate to yield alanine and α-ketoglutarate (Cahill and Owen, 1968; Felig, 1973).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cahill and Owen, 1968; Felig, 1973.

claim: The advantage of Cahill- over Cori-cycle is that reducing equivalents (i.e. NADH) gained during glycolysis are preserved.
source: The advantage of Cahill- over Cori-cycle is that reducing equivalents (i.e. NADH) gained during glycolysis are preserved and that α-ketoglutarate can yield additional ATP in mitochondrial OXPHOS.
evidence: Based on biochemical knowledge of metabolic pathways.

claim: α-ketoglutarate can yield additional ATP in mitochondrial OXPHOS.
source: The advantage of Cahill- over Cori-cycle is that reducing equivalents (i.e. NADH) gained during glycolysis are preserved and that α-ketoglutarate can yield additional ATP in mitochondrial OXPHOS.
evidence: Based on biochemical knowledge of the Krebs cycle.

claim: The mini-Krebs-cycle involves transamination of oxaloacetate with glutamate to produce aspartate and α-ketoglutarate.
source: A second alternative may be the so-called mini-Krebs-cycle, in which a transamination of oxaloacetate with glutamate produces aspartate and α-ketoglutarate (Yudkoff et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yudkoff et al., 1994.

claim: The mini-Krebs-cycle shortens the 'full' 10-step Krebs-cycle to a significantly faster 6-step cycle.
source: This shortens the 'full' 10-step Krebs-cycle to a significantly faster 6-step cycle.
evidence: Based on inference from the metabolic pathway description.

claim: Cori-, Cahill-, and mini-Krebs-cycle do not require the pyruvate-coupling between cytoplasmic glycolysis and mitochondrial OXPHOS, allowing both processes to run independent of each other.
source: A point that Cori-, Cahill-, and mini-Krebs-cycle have in common is that they do not require the pyruvate-coupling between cytoplasmic glycolysis and mitochondrial OXPHOS, allowing both processes to run independent of each other.
evidence: Based on inference from the metabolic pathway descriptions.

claim: RPE65 immunolabelling revealed the RPE cell monolayer.
source: Hence, RPE65 immunolabelling revealed the RPE cell monolayer (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Immunofluorescence for glucose transporter-1 (GLUT1) showed strong labelling on basal and apical sides of RPE cells.
source: Immunofluorescence for glucose transporter-1 (GLUT1) showed strong labelling on basal and apical sides of RPE cells (Figure 1A), in line with previous literature (Swarup et al., 2019; Takata et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1A and citations to Swarup et al., 2019; Takata et al., 1992.

claim: GLUT1 expression was not detected in rods or cones.
source: GLUT1 expression was not detected in rods or cones (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Glucose uptake in the outer retina seems to be mediated by high-affinity/high-capacity GLUT3, strongly expressed on photoreceptor inner segments.
source: Instead, glucose uptake in the outer retina seems to be mediated by high-affinity/high-capacity GLUT3 (Simpson et al., 2008), strongly expressed on photoreceptor inner segments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Simpson et al., 2008 and immunofluorescence data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: PKM2 was found in photoreceptor inner segments and synapses.
source: While pyruvate kinase M1 (PKM1) was expressed in the inner retina (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), PKM2 was found in photoreceptor inner segments and synapses (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1A.

claim: Expression of mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase (COX) largely overlapped with PKM2.
source: Expression of mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase (COX) largely overlapped with PKM2 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1A.

claim: The no RPE condition displayed significantly increased photoreceptor cell death (3.35%±1.62, n=5, p<0.001) compared to control (0.46%±0.22, n=9).
source: In control, the rate of cell death in the outer nuclear layer (ONL), as assessed by the terminal dUTP-nick-end labelling (TUNEL) assay (Figure 1C and D), was low (0.46%±0.22, n=9). The no RPE condition displayed significantly increased photoreceptor cell death (3.35%±1.62, n=5, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Blocking RPE glucose transport with 1,9-DDF further increased ONL cell death (6.77%±1.57, n=5, p<0.0001).
source: Blocking RPE glucose transport with the selective GLUT1 inhibitor 1,9-dideoxyforskolin (1,9-DDF) (Simpson et al., 2008) further increased ONL cell death (6.77%±1.57, n=5, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data and citation to Simpson et al., 2008.

claim: The inhibition of glycolytic PKM2 with Shikonin caused a significant increase in photoreceptor cell death (17.75%±2.13, n=5, p<0.0001).
source: The inhibition of glycolytic PKM2 with Shikonin (Zhao et al., 2018) and OXPHOS disruption with the electron chain uncoupler carbonyl cyanide-p-trifluoromethoxyphenylhydrazone (FCCP) (Redmond et al., 1998) both caused a significant increase in photoreceptor cell death (Shikonin: 17.75%±2.13, n=5, p<0.0001; FCCP: 22.49%±6.79, n=5, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data and citation to Zhao et al., 2018.

claim: OXPHOS disruption with FCCP caused a significant increase in photoreceptor cell death (22.49%±6.79, n=5, p<0.0001).
source: The inhibition of glycolytic PKM2 with Shikonin (Zhao et al., 2018) and OXPHOS disruption with the electron chain uncoupler carbonyl cyanide-p-trifluoromethoxyphenylhydrazone (FCCP) (Redmond et al., 1998) both caused a significant increase in photoreceptor cell death (Shikonin: 17.75%±2.13, n=5, p<0.0001; FCCP: 22.49%±6.79, n=5, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data and citation to Redmond et al., 1998.

claim: All four experimental interventions mostly affected photoreceptors, not significantly reducing the viability of other retinal cell types.
source: All four experimental interventions mostly affected photoreceptors, not significantly reducing the viability of other retinal cell types (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Control retina harboured 11.47 (±1.95, n=9) cones per 100 µm of retinal circumference.
source: Control retina harboured 11.47 (±1.95, n=9) cones per 100 µm of retinal circumference.
evidence: Supported by cone arrestin immunodetection data.

claim: no RPE retina displayed a significant decrease in cone survival (4.62±1.39, n=5, p<0.0001).
source: no RPE retina displayed a significant decrease in cone survival (4.62±1.39, n=5, p<0.0001), while blocking RPE glucose transport with 1,9-DDF led to an even more dramatic reduction (1.02±1.09, n=5, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by cone arrestin immunodetection data.

claim: Blocking RPE glucose transport with 1,9-DDF led to a dramatic reduction in cone survival (1.02±1.09, n=5, p<0.0001).
source: no RPE retina displayed a significant decrease in cone survival (4.62±1.39, n=5, p<0.0001), while blocking RPE glucose transport with 1,9-DDF led to an even more dramatic reduction (1.02±1.09, n=5, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by cone arrestin immunodetection data.

claim: Inhibition of glycolysis with Shikonin had a relatively mild effect on cone survival (7.78±1.36, n=5, p<0.0001).
source: By comparison, inhibition of glycolysis with Shikonin had a relatively mild effect on cone survival (7.78±1.36, n=5, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by cone arrestin immunodetection data.

claim: FCCP treatment did not cause cone death (12.84±1.75, n=5, p=0.22), compared to control.
source: Surprisingly, FCCP treatment did not cause cone death (12.84±1.75, n=5, p=0.22), compared to control.
evidence: Supported by cone arrestin immunodetection data.

claim: 3% of all photoreceptors are cones.
source: We further calculated the percentages of dying cones and rods, assuming that 3% of all photoreceptors were cones (Ortín-Martínez et al., 2014; Jeon et al., 1998; Figure 1G and H).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ortín-Martínez et al., 2014; Jeon et al., 1998.

claim: Cones were almost entirely depleted by the 1,9-DDF treatment but remained virtually unaffected by the FCCP treatment.
source: Cones were almost entirely depleted by the 1,9-DDF treatment but remained virtually unaffected by the FCCP treatment.
evidence: Supported by cone survival data from Figure 1E-H.

claim: Rods were strongly and highly selectively affected by Shikonin and FCCP.
source: Rods, however, were strongly and highly selectively affected by Shikonin and FCCP, while the no RPE condition had a relatively minor effect.
evidence: Inferred from cell death data and cone survival data in Figure 1.

claim: These results highlight important differences between rod and cone energy metabolism.
source: These results highlight important differences between rod and cone energy metabolism.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from differential effects of treatments on rods and cones.

claim: A principal component analysis showed clear group separation among the five experimental groups.
source: A principal component analysis showed clear group separation (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by PCA data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The greatest cluster overlap was seen in control and Shikonin groups.
source: The greatest cluster overlap was seen in control and Shikonin groups.
evidence: Supported by hierarchical clustering analysis in Figure 2A.

claim: Glutamate, aspartate, alanine, O-phosphocholine, and NAD+ concentrations were particularly upregulated in the 1,9-DDF condition compared to control.
source: We found the strongest changes in the 1,9-DDF condition, where glutamate, aspartate, alanine, O-phosphocholine, and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) concentrations were particularly upregulated compared to control.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Figure 2A.

claim: Branched chain amino acids (BCAAs), lactate, and threonine were upregulated in the FCCP and no RPE condition.
source: Further, branched chain amino acids (BCAAs), lactate, and threonine were upregulated in the FCCP and no RPE condition.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Figure 2A.

claim: Glutathione (GSH) and glutathione disulfide (GSSG) were relatively reduced by Shikonin treatment, with increased creatine and formate.
source: Glutathione (GSH) and glutathione disulfide (GSSG) were relatively reduced by Shikonin treatment, with increased creatine and formate.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Figure 2A.

claim: Control and 1,9-DDF treatment displayed high levels of GTP, ATP, and π-methylhistidine, which were low in the other groups.
source: Control and 1,9-DDF treatment displayed high levels of guanosine triphosphate (GTP), ATP, and π-methylhistidine, which were low in the other groups (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Figure 2A.

claim: The energy charge appeared to be reduced in the Shikonin and FCCP condition.
source: The energy charge appeared to be reduced in the Shikonin and FCCP condition, while the GSH/GSSG ratio of the tissue was not significantly changed from control in any condition (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by energy charge calculations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The GSH/GSSG ratio of the tissue was not significantly changed from control in any condition.
source: The energy charge appeared to be reduced in the Shikonin and FCCP condition, while the GSH/GSSG ratio of the tissue was not significantly changed from control in any condition (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by GSH/GSSG ratio data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: 1,9-DDF treatment reduced glucose consumption compared to control.
source: As could be expected, 1,9-DDF treatment reduced glucose consumption compared to control, while FCCP treatment increased glucose expenditure (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by glucose concentration measurements in spent medium shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: FCCP treatment increased glucose expenditure.
source: As could be expected, 1,9-DDF treatment reduced glucose consumption compared to control, while FCCP treatment increased glucose expenditure (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by glucose concentration measurements in spent medium shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Lactate production was decreased in the 1,9-DDF group.
source: Conversely, lactate production was decreased in the 1,9-DDF group. However, in the no RPE condition and after FCCP treatment lactate concentrations in the spent medium were strongly and significantly elevated (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by lactate concentration measurements in spent medium shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: In the no RPE condition and after FCCP treatment lactate concentrations in the spent medium were strongly and significantly elevated.
source: Conversely, lactate production was decreased in the 1,9-DDF group. However, in the no RPE condition and after FCCP treatment lactate concentrations in the spent medium were strongly and significantly elevated (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by lactate concentration measurements in spent medium shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The metabolite profile of control was markedly different from retina cultured without RPE, with 25 metabolites exhibiting significant changes.
source: The metabolite profile of control was markedly different from retina cultured without RPE, with 25 metabolites exhibiting significant changes (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Decreased ATP levels in the no RPE group corresponded to increased lactate.
source: Decreased ATP levels in the no RPE group corresponded to increased lactate.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Figure 3A.

claim: The BCAAs isoleucine, leucine, and valine, and some of the glucogenic/ketogenic AAs threonine, methionine, glycine, displayed higher levels in the no RPE group compared to control.
source: The BCAAs isoleucine, leucine, and valine, and some of the glucogenic/ketogenic AAs threonine, methionine, glycine, displayed higher levels in the no RPE group compared to control.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Alanine, aspartate, and taurine showed lower levels in the no RPE group compared to control.
source: Alanine, aspartate, and taurine showed the opposite trend.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Figure 3A.

claim: Hypotaurine, 4-aminobutyrate (GABA), and glutamate were accumulated in retinal tissue in the no RPE condition.
source: Hypotaurine, 4-aminobutyrate (GABA), and glutamate were accumulated in retinal tissue, while membrane synthesis-associated metabolites, such as myo-inositol and O-phosphocholine, as well as creatine and N-acetylaspartate (NAA) were reduced in neuroretina.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Figure 3A.

claim: Membrane synthesis-associated metabolites, such as myo-inositol and O-phosphocholine, as well as creatine and NAA were reduced in neuroretina in the no RPE condition.
source: Hypotaurine, 4-aminobutyrate (GABA), and glutamate were accumulated in retinal tissue, while membrane synthesis-associated metabolites, such as myo-inositol and O-phosphocholine, as well as creatine and N-acetylaspartate (NAA) were reduced in neuroretina.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Figure 3A.

claim: Higher levels of GSSG appeared in the absence of RPE, pointing towards an altered redox metabolism.
source: Moreover, higher levels of GSSG appeared in the absence of RPE, pointing towards an altered redox metabolism.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Figure 3A and inference about redox state.

claim: Citrate positively correlated with taurine, alanine, aspartate, and ATP.
source: Pattern hunter (Pearson r) correlation analysis found citrate, a central Krebs-cycle metabolite, positively correlated with taurine, alanine, aspartate, and ATP (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by pattern hunter correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Citrate negatively correlated with ADP, BCAAs, and lactate.
source: Negative correlations with citrate included ADP, BCAAs, and lactate.
evidence: Supported by pattern hunter correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: KEGG-based pathway analysis revealed changes in arginine and proline metabolism, taurine and hypotaurine metabolism, and alanine, aspartate, and glutamate metabolism in the no RPE situation.
source: A subsequent Kyoto Encyclopaedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG)-based pathway analysis revealed changes in arginine and proline metabolism, taurine and hypotaurine metabolism, and alanine, aspartate, and glutamate metabolism in the no RPE situation (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Citrate synthase (CS) and fumarase were found mostly in photoreceptor inner segments and synaptic terminals.
source: Citrate synthase (CS) and fumarase, key enzymes of the Krebs-cycle, were found mostly in photoreceptor inner segments and synaptic terminals.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3D.

claim: The γ-subunit of ATP synthase was localised to photoreceptor inner segments and synapses.
source: The γ-subunit of ATP synthase, essential for OXPHOS, was also localised to photoreceptor inner segments and synapses.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3D.

claim: Low ATP levels in the no RPE group likely resulted from decreased photoreceptor Krebs-cycle and OXPHOS activity.
source: Thus, low ATP levels in the no RPE group likely resulted from decreased photoreceptor Krebs-cycle and OXPHOS activity.
evidence: Inferred from enzyme localization and metabolomics data.

claim: High levels of taurine were detected in photoreceptor inner segments and synapses, as well as in the ganglion cell layer.
source: High levels of taurine were detected in photoreceptor inner segments and synapses, as well as in the ganglion cell layer (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3D.

claim: The enzyme alanine transaminase (ALT) was found to be expressed in the inner nuclear and plexiform layers.
source: Finally, the enzyme alanine transaminase (ALT), previously thought to be expressed only in muscle and liver, was found to be expressed in the inner nuclear and plexiform layers (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3D.

claim: ALT was strongly expressed in cone inner segments.
source: ALT was also strongly expressed in cone inner segments, as evidenced by co-labelling with cone-Arr3.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence co-labeling data in Figure 3D.

claim: The ALT expression pattern and high alanine levels in the control strongly suggested Cahill-cycle activity in the retina.
source: This expression pattern and high alanine levels in the control strongly suggested Cahill-cycle activity in the retina (Felig, 1973).
evidence: Inferred from enzyme expression and metabolite data, with citation to Felig, 1973.

claim: When ALT activity was inhibited with β-chloro-alanine, photoreceptor cell death was increased and cone survival was reduced.
source: When ALT activity was inhibited with β-chloro-alanine, photoreceptor cell death was increased and notably cone survival was reduced, functionally validating the expression of ALT in the outer retina (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The accumulation of BCAA, glutamate, and lactate, concomitant with decreased alanine levels in the no RPE group, implied that RPE removal switched retinal metabolism from Krebs-cycle/OXPHOS to aerobic glycolysis.
source: Notably, the accumulation of BCAA, glutamate, and lactate, concomitant with decreased alanine levels in the no RPE group, implied that RPE removal switched retinal metabolism from Krebs-cycle/OXPHOS to aerobic glycolysis.
evidence: Inferred from metabolomics data patterns.

claim: The no RPE and FCCP groups showed similar metabolite patterns and pathway changes overall.
source: Since in Figure 2, the no RPE and FCCP groups showed similar metabolite patterns and pathway changes overall, we subjected these two experimental groups to a detailed statistical analysis.
evidence: Observed from metabolomics data in Figure 2.

claim: Detailed statistical analysis revealed 17 significant metabolite changes between no RPE and FCCP groups.
source: This revealed 17 significant metabolite changes (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: GTP was among the most highly reduced metabolite concentrations in the FCCP group.
source: Among the most highly reduced metabolite concentrations in the FCCP group was GTP, which positively correlated with GABA, ATP, GSSG, hypotaurine, and NAD+ (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Figure 4A.

claim: GTP positively correlated with GABA, ATP, GSSG, hypotaurine, and NAD+.
source: Among the most highly reduced metabolite concentrations in the FCCP group was GTP, which positively correlated with GABA, ATP, GSSG, hypotaurine, and NAD+ (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by pattern hunter correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: GDP, BCAAs, glutamine, and citrate negatively correlated to GTP.
source: In contrast, GDP, BCAAs, glutamine, and citrate negatively correlated to GTP.
evidence: Supported by pattern hunter correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: KEGG-based pathway analysis ranked glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism, GSH metabolism, and alanine, aspartate, and glutamate metabolism as the most significantly changed between no RPE and FCCP conditions.
source: The KEGG-based pathway analysis ranked glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism, GSH metabolism, and alanine, aspartate, and glutamate metabolism as the most significantly changed between the two conditions (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Measurable amounts of GTP can only be generated by succinate-CoA ligase, GTP-forming-1 (SUCLG-1) in the Krebs-cycle, or from excess ATP by nucleoside-diphosphate kinase.
source: Curiously, measurable amounts of GTP can only be generated in two ways: (1) by succinate-CoA ligase, GTP-forming-1 (SUCLG-1) in the Krebs-cycle, and (2) from excess ATP by nucleoside-diphosphate kinase, an enzyme expressed in photoreceptor inner and outer segments (Abdulaev et al., 1998; Rueda et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on biochemical knowledge with citations to Abdulaev et al., 1998; Rueda et al., 2016.

claim: Since ATP levels were low in both the FCCP and the no RPE situation, GTP could not have been produced from ATP.
source: Since ATP levels were low in both the FCCP and the no RPE situation, here, GTP could not have been produced from ATP.
evidence: Inferred from metabolomics data showing low ATP levels.

claim: SUCLG-1 showed strong expression in photoreceptor inner segments and synapses, where it co-localised to a large extent with mitochondrial COX.
source: Immunofluorescence for SUCLG-1 showed strong expression in photoreceptor inner segments and synapses, where it co-localised to a large extent with mitochondrial COX (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4D.

claim: The SUCLG-1 retinal expression pattern and the synthesis of GTP in the absence of RPE provided clear evidence for Krebs-cycle activity in photoreceptors.
source: Hence, the SUCLG-1 retinal expression pattern and the synthesis of GTP in the absence of RPE provided clear evidence for Krebs-cycle activity in photoreceptors.
evidence: Inferred from enzyme expression and metabolite data.

claim: FCCP-induced upregulation of citrate, concomitant with a downregulation of NAD+, indicated a Krebs-cycle interruption at the level of D-isocitrate to α-ketoglutarate conversion.
source: We also identified an FCCP-induced upregulation of citrate, concomitant with a downregulation of NAD+. This indicated a Krebs-cycle interruption at the level of D-isocitrate to α-ketoglutarate conversion, i.e., a step that requires NAD+.
evidence: Inferred from metabolomics data and biochemical knowledge.

claim: NAD+ is consumed by poly-ADP-ribose-polymerase (PARP), which is activated by oxidative DNA damage.
source: NAD+ is known to be consumed by poly-ADP-ribose-polymerase (PARP), which is activated by oxidative DNA damage (Bai, 2015) and upregulated in dying photoreceptors (Paquet-Durand et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bai, 2015 and Paquet-Durand et al., 2007.

claim: Compared to the no RPE group, more photoreceptor cells in the FCCP-treated retina showed PAR accumulation, correlating with decreased retinal NAD+ levels.
source: Compared to the no RPE group, more photoreceptor cells in the FCCP-treated retina showed PAR accumulation, correlating with decreased retinal NAD+ levels (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: Supported by PAR immunodetection and NAD+ measurements shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: FCCP-induced oxidative stress may cause increased PARP activity and decreased NAD+ levels, eventually interrupting the Krebs-cycle, as evidenced by citrate accumulation.
source: Hence, FCCP-induced oxidative stress may cause increased PARP activity and decreased NAD+ levels, eventually interrupting the Krebs-cycle, as evidenced by citrate accumulation.
evidence: Inferred from PAR, NAD+, and citrate data.

claim: Disruption of OXPHOS led to AA accumulation, including lysine, phenylalanine, glutamine, leucine, and valine.
source: Overall, the data from the no RPE to FCCP group comparison showed that disruption of OXPHOS led to AA accumulation, including lysine, phenylalanine, glutamine, leucine, and valine.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data comparing no RPE and FCCP groups.

claim: Alanine accumulation in the FCCP group was likely caused by ALT-dependent pyruvate transamination.
source: Notably, alanine accumulation in the FCCP group was likely caused by ALT-dependent pyruvate transamination.
evidence: Inferred from metabolomics data and ALT expression.

claim: Metabolites high in the no RPE group but low with FCCP treatment were probably related to Krebs-cycle in the neuroretina, especially GTP, aspartate, and NAA.
source: By contrast, metabolites high in the no RPE group but low with FCCP treatment were probably related to Krebs-cycle in the neuroretina. This concerned especially GTP, aspartate, and NAA.
evidence: Inferred from metabolomics data patterns.

claim: The metabolic response to 1,9-DDF treatment was very different from the no RPE situation.
source: Since GLUT1 was predominantly expressed in the RPE, we initially assumed that the metabolic response to 1,9-DDF treatment might resemble that of the no RPE situation. However, the patterns found between these two groups were very different (Figure 2) and to explore these differences further, we performed an additional two-way comparison.
evidence: Observed from metabolomics data in Figure 2.

claim: Comparison of no RPE and 1,9-DDF groups revealed 28 significantly changed metabolites.
source: This analysis revealed 28 significantly changed metabolites (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: When compared to the no RPE, the 1,9-DDF group showed changes in mitochondria and Krebs-cycle-associated metabolites (e.g. high ATP, high formate, low BCAA).
source: When compared to the no RPE, the 1,9-DDF group showed changes in mitochondria and Krebs-cycle-associated metabolites (e.g. high ATP, high formate, low BCAA).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Figure 5A.

claim: The Cahill-cycle product alanine and NAA were upregulated by 1,9-DDF treatment.
source: Conversely, the Cahill-cycle product alanine and NAA were upregulated by 1,9-DDF treatment.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Figure 5A.

claim: Metabolites formate, glutamate, taurine, and citrate were positively correlated with ATP.
source: The pattern hunter analysis showed that metabolites formate, glutamate, taurine, and citrate were positively correlated with ATP, while, AMP, GMP, and BCAA were negatively correlated with ATP (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by pattern hunter correlation analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: AMP, GMP, and BCAA were negatively correlated with ATP.
source: The pattern hunter analysis showed that metabolites formate, glutamate, taurine, and citrate were positively correlated with ATP, while, AMP, GMP, and BCAA were negatively correlated with ATP (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by pattern hunter correlation analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: KEGG pathway analysis showed alanine, aspartate, and glutamate metabolism, GSH metabolism and glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism among the three most affected pathways in the no RPE vs 1,9-DDF comparison.
source: The KEGG pathway analysis showed alanine, aspartate, and glutamate metabolism, GSH metabolism and glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism among the three most affected pathways (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The depletion of BCAAs in the 1,9-DDF treatment indicated that either the RPE, the neuroretina, or both used anaplerotic substrates to fuel the Krebs-cycle and maintain ATP production.
source: Taken together, the depletion of BCAAs in the 1,9-DDF treatment indicated that either the RPE, the neuroretina, or both used anaplerotic substrates to fuel the Krebs-cycle and maintain ATP production.
evidence: Inferred from metabolomics data showing BCAA depletion and high ATP.

claim: The Shikonin vs FCCP comparison showed increased formate, aspartate, and NAA levels in the Shikonin group.
source: This analysis showed increased formate, aspartate, and NAA levels in the Shikonin group (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Figure 5C.

claim: Higher amounts of GSH, GSSG, BCAA, threonine, and phenylalanine after FCCP treatment indicated Krebs-cycle interruption.
source: Conversely, higher amounts of GSH, GSSG, BCAA, threonine, and phenylalanine after FCCP treatment indicated Krebs-cycle interruption (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Inferred from metabolomics data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The production of lactate was higher with FCCP compared to Shikonin treatment, probably reflecting increased glycolysis to compensate for the loss of Krebs-cycle-dependent ATP production.
source: The production of lactate was higher with FCCP compared to Shikonin treatment, probably reflecting increased glycolysis to compensate for the loss of Krebs-cycle-dependent ATP production.
evidence: Inferred from metabolomics data.

claim: Metabolites connected to oxidative stress, such as GSSG and GSH, were increased by FCCP treatment.
source: Metabolites connected to oxidative stress, such as GSSG and GSH, were also increased by FCCP treatment.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data.

claim: Pattern hunter for metabolites correlated with GSH found 3-hydroxyisovalerate, glutamine, GSSG, lactate and ATP positively correlated, while succinate, alanine, and GABA were negatively correlated with GSH.
source: Pattern hunter for metabolites correlated with GSH found 3-hydroxyisovalerate, glutamine, GSSG, but also lactate and ATP, while succinate, alanine, and GABA were negatively correlated with GSH (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by pattern hunter correlation analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Pathway analysis identified arginine biosynthesis, alanine, aspartate, and glutamate metabolism, as well as glycolysis and gluconeogenesis as the most strongly regulated metabolic pathways in the Shikonin vs FCCP comparison.
source: The subsequent pathway analysis identified arginine biosynthesis, alanine, aspartate, and glutamate metabolism, as well as glycolysis and gluconeogenesis as the most strongly regulated metabolic pathways (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The treatment with 1,9-DDF resulted in near-complete cone loss, while cones were fully preserved with FCCP treatment.
source: The treatment with 1,9-DDF resulted in near-complete cone loss, while cones were fully preserved with FCCP treatment (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by cone survival data in Figure 1.

claim: Three-way comparison revealed 29 metabolite concentrations that were significantly changed.
source: In this three-way comparison, 29 metabolite concentrations were significantly changed (Figure 6A; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The FCCP treatment reduced ATP and GTP levels, while lactate production was greatly increased, along with methionine and threonine.
source: The FCCP treatment reduced ATP and GTP levels, while lactate production was greatly increased, along with methionine and threonine.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Figure 6A.

claim: BCAAs, glutamine, phenylalanine, and tyrosine showed a significant upregulation with FCCP treatment.
source: BCAAs, glutamine, phenylalanine, and tyrosine also showed a significant upregulation with FCCP treatment.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Figure 6A.

claim: Some metabolites like GSSG, serine, glutamate, alanine, NAD+, and taurine displayed a pronounced increase in the 1,9-DDF group when compared to either control or FCCP.
source: Interestingly, some metabolites like GSSG, serine, glutamate, alanine, NAD+, and taurine displayed a pronounced increase in the 1,9-DDF group when compared to either control or FCCP.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Figure 6A.

claim: Formate, aspartate, and myo-inositol were upregulated with 1,9-DDF treatment, together with NAA and creatine.
source: In addition, formate, aspartate, and myo-inositol were upregulated with 1,9-DDF treatment, together with NAA and creatine.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Figure 6A.

claim: The comparison between the 1,9-DDF and FCCP groups revealed highly increased levels of ATP and GTP, implying a strong activation of the Krebs-cycle under 1,9-DDF treatment.
source: Finally, the comparison between the 1,9-DDF and FCCP groups revealed highly increased levels of ATP and GTP, implying a strong activation of the Krebs-cycle under 1,9-DDF treatment.
evidence: Inferred from metabolomics data in Figure 6A.

claim: BCAAs and tyrosine exhibited low levels in the rod-rich 1,9-DDF group and high levels in the cone-rich FCCP group, indicating that these metabolites might be consumed by rods or produced in cones.
source: BCAAs and tyrosine (and glutamine) exhibited low levels in the rod-rich 1,9-DDF group and high levels in the cone-rich FCCP group, indicating that these metabolites might be consumed by rods or produced in cones.
evidence: Inferred from metabolomics data patterns and differential cell survival.

claim: Aspartate and NAA were predominantly produced in rods.
source: Vice versa, it may be assumed that aspartate and NAA were predominantly produced in rods.
evidence: Inferred from metabolomics data patterns and differential cell survival.

claim: Glutamine synthase (GS) is strongly expressed in MGCs.
source: We confirmed a strong expression of glutamine synthase (GS) in MGCs (Riepe and Norenburg, 1977).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6B and citation to Riepe and Norenburg, 1977.

claim: Glutaminase C (GAC) was prominently expressed in photoreceptor inner segments, photoreceptor synapses, and INL.
source: Remarkably, the enzyme that hydrolyses glutamine to glutamate, glutaminase C (GAC) was prominently expressed in photoreceptor inner segments, photoreceptor synapses, and INL.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6B.

claim: GAC showed strong expression in cone inner segments.
source: Co-labelling with cone Arr3 revealed a strong expression of GAC in cone inner segments, implying that cones could use glutamine as a metabolic substrate.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence co-labeling data in Figure 6B.

claim: Treatment with the GAC-specific inhibitor Compound 968 dose-dependently reduced photoreceptor viability – affecting cones more strongly than rods – while leaving the inner retina mostly intact.
source: Accordingly, treatment with the GAC-specific inhibitor Compound 968 dose-dependently reduced photoreceptor viability – affecting cones more strongly than rods – while leaving the inner retina mostly intact (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: In the no RPE group, the GTP to lactate ratio was significantly lower than in control, indicating 4.1 times higher glycolytic activity.
source: In the no RPE group, the GTP to lactate ratio was significantly lower than in control, indicating 4.1 times higher glycolytic activity.
evidence: Calculated from metabolomics data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: With FCCP treatment the GTP to lactate ratio dropped to the lowest level, in line with a strong downregulation of Krebs-cycle and concomitant upregulation of glycolysis.
source: While in the 1,9-DDF and Shikonin group the GTP to lactate ratios were not significantly different from control, with FCCP treatment this ratio dropped to the lowest level, in line with a strong downregulation of Krebs-cycle and concomitant upregulation of glycolysis.
evidence: Calculated from metabolomics data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Under control conditions, and in the no RPE and FCCP groups, serine synthesis pathway activity was rather low, while it was strongly increased by 1,9-DDF and Shikonin treatment.
source: We then calculated the ratio of serine to lactate as an indicator for serine synthesis pathway activity. Under control conditions, and in the no RPE and FCCP groups, this activity was rather low, while it was strongly increased by 1,9-DDF and Shikonin treatment.
evidence: Calculated from metabolomics data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In the Shikonin group, serine production from 3-phosphoglycerate and subsequent deamination to pyruvate may bypass the PKM2 block.
source: In the Shikonin group, serine production from 3-phosphoglycerate and subsequent deamination to pyruvate may bypass the PKM2 block.
evidence: Inferred from metabolomics data and biochemical knowledge.

claim: A comparatively low GTP to BCAA ratio in the no RPE situation showed that much of the GTP generated in the neuroretina likely came from anaplerotic substrates.
source: Finally, we used the ratio of GTP to BCAAs to investigate to what extent Krebs-cycle activity was driven by anaplerotic metabolism. A comparatively low GTP to BCAA ratio in the no RPE situation showed that much of the GTP generated in the neuroretina likely came from anaplerotic substrates.
evidence: Calculated from metabolomics data shown in Figure 6C and inferred.

claim: Both Shikonin and FCCP treatment decreased BCAA use.
source: While both Shikonin and FCCP treatment decreased BCAA use, 1,9-DDF treatment increased anaplerotic metabolism.
evidence: Calculated from metabolomics data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: 1,9-DDF treatment increased anaplerotic metabolism.
source: While both Shikonin and FCCP treatment decreased BCAA use, 1,9-DDF treatment increased anaplerotic metabolism.
evidence: Calculated from metabolomics data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: A large proportion of the GTP produced in the neuroretina by SUCLG-1 was derived from anaplerotic substrates rather than from pyruvate in the no RPE situation.
source: Comparing the ratios of GTP to lactate with GTP to BCAA in the no RPE situation showed that a large proportion of the GTP produced in the neuroretina by SUCLG-1 was derived from anaplerotic substrates rather than from pyruvate.
evidence: Inferred from metabolite ratio calculations.

claim: The neuroretinal Krebs-cycle might not start with citrate but instead only an α-ketoglutarate to oxaloacetate shunt would be employed, including the GTP-synthesising step from succinyl-CoA to succinate.
source: These substrates enter the Krebs-cycle mostly at the level of α-ketoglutarate, suggesting that the neuroretinal Krebs-cycle might not start with citrate. Instead, only an α-ketoglutarate to oxaloacetate shunt would be employed, including the GTP-synthesising step from succinyl-CoA to succinate (Figure 7A).
evidence: Inferred from metabolomics data and illustrated in Figure 7A.

claim: A key step of the mini-Krebs-cycle is the transamination of oxaloacetate with glutamate by aspartate aminotransferase (AST) to yield α-ketoglutarate and aspartate, which is further acetylated to NAA.
source: A key step of this mini-Krebs-cycle (Riepe and Norenburg, 1977) is the transamination of oxaloacetate with glutamate by aspartate aminotransferase (AST) to yield α-ketoglutarate and aspartate, which is further acetylated to NAA.
evidence: Based on biochemical knowledge with citation to Riepe and Norenburg, 1977.

claim: Hierarchical clustering showed similar patterns for aspartate and NAA in all experimental conditions.
source: Hierarchical clustering showed similar patterns for aspartate and NAA in all experimental conditions (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Except for the FCCP treatment, the ratio of citrate/NAA was 0.5, indicating that the retina preferred the mini-Krebs-cycle over the full Krebs-cycle.
source: Except for the FCCP treatment, the ratio of citrate/NAA was 0.5, indicating that the retina preferred the mini-Krebs-cycle over the full Krebs-cycle (Figure 7C).
evidence: Calculated from metabolomics data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Both AST1 and AST2 were expressed in photoreceptor inner segments and cell bodies.
source: Immunolabelling for AST – conventionally associated with muscle and liver metabolism (Nathwani et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2008) – found both AST1 and AST2 to be expressed in photoreceptor inner segments and cell bodies (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 7D and citations to Nathwani et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2008.

claim: Photoreceptors can execute the mini-Krebs-cycle, while the NAA production seen in the metabolomic data suggested that this cycle was indeed used.
source: This confirmed that photoreceptors can execute the mini-Krebs-cycle, while the NAA production seen in the metabolomic data suggested that this cycle was indeed used (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from enzyme expression and metabolomics data.

claim: Using anaplerotic substrates the Cahill- and mini-Krebs cycles allow for far more efficient energy production compared to the Cori-cycle.
source: Using anaplerotic substrates the Cahill- and mini-Krebs cycles allow for far more efficient energy production compared to the Cori-cycle.
evidence: Based on biochemical calculations shown in Figure 8.

claim: The mini-Krebs-cycle may deliver up to 18 moles of ATP and 2 moles of GTP per 3 carbon unit, exceeding the 15 moles of ATP and 1 mole of GTP generated in the 'full' Krebs-cycle.
source: Assuming that 1 mole of NADH/FADH2 can be used to generate 3 moles of ATP via OXPHOS, and depending on the exact stoichiometry of glutamate/BCAA input, the mini-Krebs-cycle may deliver up to 18 moles of ATP and 2 moles of GTP per 3 carbon unit. Astonishingly, this exceeds the 15 moles of ATP and 1 mole of GTP generated in the 'full' Krebs-cycle.
evidence: Based on biochemical calculations shown in Figure 8.

claim: Photoreceptors are able to uncouple glycolysis and Krebs-cycle using an NAA-producing shunt.
source: Importantly, we show that photoreceptors are able to uncouple glycolysis and Krebs-cycle using an NAA-producing shunt.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from metabolomics and enzyme expression data.

claim: The high rates of retinal aerobic glycolysis first reported by Otto Warburg are likely an artefact of the absence of RPE, while intact retina may rely more on OXPHOS for its energy production.
source: Taken together, the high rates of retinal aerobic glycolysis first reported by Otto Warburg are likely an artefact of the absence of RPE, while intact retina may rely more on OXPHOS for its energy production.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparing metabolomics data with and without RPE.

claim: FCCP eliminates the proton gradient between inner mitochondrial membrane and mitochondrial matrix, abolishing ATP synthesis.
source: FCCP eliminates the proton gradient between inner mitochondrial membrane and mitochondrial matrix, abolishing ATP synthesis (Kessler et al., 1976).
evidence: Based on established knowledge with citation to Kessler et al., 1976.

claim: FCCP may increase Krebs-cycle activity to attempt restoration of mitochondrial proton gradient, increasing oxidative stress and oxidative DNA damage.
source: Initially, FCCP may increase Krebs-cycle activity to attempt restoration of mitochondrial proton gradient (Balcke et al., 2011), increasing oxidative stress (Dugan et al., 1995), and oxidative DNA damage.
evidence: Based on inference with citations to Balcke et al., 2011 and Dugan et al., 1995.

claim: The resultant activation of PARP would deplete NAD+, further aggravating metabolic stress.
source: The resultant activation of PARP would deplete NAD+, further aggravating metabolic stress (Schreiber et al., 2006).
evidence: Based on inference with citation to Schreiber et al., 2006.

claim: Glycolysis is sufficient and necessary for cone survival.
source: These differential effects of FCCP and 1,9-DDF treatments strongly suggest that glycolysis is sufficient and necessary for cone survival, in agreement with earlier studies who showed that under stress cones require glycolysis to remain viable (Venkatesh et al., 2015; Aït-Ali et al., 2015).
evidence: Inferred from differential treatment effects with citations to Venkatesh et al., 2015; Aït-Ali et al., 2015.

claim: Rods require OXPHOS for their survival, while glycolysis is of minor importance.
source: Conversely, rods require OXPHOS for their survival, while glycolysis is of minor importance.
evidence: Inferred from differential treatment effects on rods.

claim: An intact blood-retinal barrier and regulation of glucose access was important for cone survival.
source: Furthermore, cone viability relative to rods was also strongly compromised in the no RPE situation, indicating that an intact blood-retinal barrier (O'Leary and Campbell, 2023) and regulation of glucose access was important for cone survival.
evidence: Inferred from cone survival data with citation to O'Leary and Campbell, 2023.

claim: RPE cells express high levels of GLUT1, while photoreceptors express the neuronal glucose transporter GLUT3.
source: Our work shows that RPE cells express high levels of GLUT1, while photoreceptors express the neuronal glucose transporter GLUT3.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: GLUT2 may contribute to photoreceptor glucose uptake indirectly via horizontal cells.
source: Furthermore, GLUT2 may contribute to photoreceptor glucose uptake indirectly via horizontal cells (Yang et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2022.

claim: In the brain, low-affinity GLUT1 (Km = 6.9 mM) is expressed on glial cells, which contact blood vessels, while high-affinity GLUT3 (Km = 1.8 mM) is expressed on neurons.
source: In the brain the generally accepted setup for GLUT1 and GLUT3 expression is that low-affinity GLUT1 (Km = 6.9 mM) is expressed on glial cells, which contact blood vessels, while high-affinity GLUT3 (Km = 1.8 mM) is expressed on neurons (Burant and Bell, 1992; Koepsell, 2020).
evidence: Based on established knowledge with citations to Burant and Bell, 1992; Koepsell, 2020.

claim: The lactate-generating Cori-cycle is highly inefficient and in intact retina likely plays a lesser role.
source: The lactate-generating Cori-cycle (Cori and Cori, 1946) is highly inefficient and in intact retina likely plays a lesser role.
evidence: Based on biochemical knowledge and metabolomics data with citation to Cori and Cori, 1946.

claim: The expression of mitochondrial PCK2 in cones facilitates the efficient uncoupling of glycolysis from the Krebs-cycle, suggesting that cones may use the Cahill-cycle for very effective energy production.
source: Moreover, the expression of mitochondrial PCK2 in cones facilitates the efficient uncoupling of glycolysis from the Krebs-cycle, suggesting that cones may use the Cahill-cycle for very effective energy production.
evidence: Inferred from enzyme expression data in Figure 6B.

claim: Cones might be able to use the serine-synthesis pathway to bypass the Shikonin block of PKM2.
source: In this situation, cones might be able to use the serine-synthesis pathway – with serine production from 3-phosphoglycerate and subsequent deamination to pyruvate – to bypass the Shikonin block of PKM2.
evidence: Speculative inference from metabolomics data.

claim: Retinal has been proposed to form a Schiff base adduct with taurine, which would act as a retinal carrier and buffer.
source: Recently, retinal has been proposed to form a Schiff base adduct with taurine, which would act as a retinal carrier and buffer (Veeravalli et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Veeravalli et al., 2020.

claim: Taurine has been suggested to be an important osmolyte in the retina that may flow in and out of neuronal cells in response to neuronal activity.
source: Moreover, taurine has been suggested to be an important osmolyte in the retina that may flow in and out of neuronal cells in response to neuronal activity (Ripps and Shen, 2012; Pasantes-Morales et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ripps and Shen, 2012; Pasantes-Morales et al., 1999.

claim: Retina cultured with RPE harboured high levels of taurine and low levels of hypotaurine, while retina without RPE displayed low levels of taurine and high levels of hypotaurine.
source: We found that retina cultured with RPE harboured high levels of taurine and low levels of hypotaurine, while retina without RPE displayed low levels of taurine and high levels of hypotaurine.
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data.

claim: Taurine immunostaining found essentially no taurine in the RPE, while photoreceptor inner segments and synapses displayed very high taurine levels.
source: Our taurine immunostaining found essentially no taurine in the RPE, while photoreceptor inner segments and synapses displayed very high taurine levels.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3D.

claim: These findings suggest a hypotaurine-taurine shuttle between RPE and photoreceptors.
source: Together, these findings suggest a hypotaurine-taurine shuttle between RPE and photoreceptors.
evidence: Inferred from metabolomics and immunofluorescence data.

claim: In the RPE taurine can be reduced to hypotaurine and shuttled back to photoreceptors where oxidation by hypotaurine dehydrogenase may reconstitute taurine, yielding additional NADH for OXPHOS.
source: In the RPE taurine can be reduced to hypotaurine and shuttled back to photoreceptors where oxidation by hypotaurine dehydrogenase (Veeravalli et al., 2020; Sumizu, 1962) may reconstitute taurine, yielding additional NADH for OXPHOS.
evidence: Speculative model based on metabolomics data with citations to Veeravalli et al., 2020; Sumizu, 1962.

claim: The net effect of the hypotaurine-taurine shuttle would be a transfer of reducing power from RPE to photoreceptors, boosting photoreceptor ATP production via OXPHOS.
source: The net effect of this hypotaurine-taurine shuttle would be a transfer of reducing power from RPE to photoreceptors, boosting photoreceptor ATP production via OXPHOS.
evidence: Speculative inference from proposed shuttle mechanism.

claim: Hypotaurine-taurine shuttling will have an impact on the osmolarity of both photoreceptors and RPE cells.
source: In addition, it seems likely that hypotaurine-taurine shuttling will have an impact on the osmolarity of both photoreceptors and RPE cells.
evidence: Speculative inference from proposed shuttle mechanism.

claim: Pyruvate coupling is especially problematic in high and rapidly changing energy demand such as in neurons and photoreceptors.
source: Pyruvate coupling is especially problematic in high and rapidly changing energy demand such as in neurons and photoreceptors (Du et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on inference with citation to Du et al., 2016.

claim: Uncoupling glycolysis and Krebs-cycle via the Cori-cycle is extremely wasteful and likely insufficient to satisfy long-term photoreceptor energy demand.
source: Uncoupling glycolysis and Krebs-cycle via the Cori-cycle is extremely wasteful and likely insufficient to satisfy long-term photoreceptor energy demand.
evidence: Based on biochemical knowledge and inference.

claim: The Cahill-cycle delivers additional NADH when using pyruvate derived from glycolysis, and cones may use the Cahill-cycle for uncoupling from glycolysis.
source: By comparison, the Cahill-cycle delivers additional NADH when using pyruvate derived from glycolysis, and cones may use the Cahill-cycle for uncoupling from glycolysis.
evidence: Inferred from metabolomics and enzyme expression data.

claim: The mini-Krebs-cycle is used primarily by rods, perhaps explaining their selective vulnerability to FCCP treatment.
source: We found mitochondrial AST2 to be expressed in rod inner segments, in agreement with an early cytochemical study (Gebhard, 1991). This indicates that the mini-Krebs-cycle is used primarily by rods, perhaps explaining their selective vulnerability to FCCP treatment.
evidence: Inferred from enzyme expression data with citation to Gebhard, 1991.

claim: The mini-Krebs-cycle is more energy-efficient than the Cahill-cycle and generates NAA instead of alanine as net product.
source: Crucially, the mini-Krebs-cycle is more energy-efficient than the Cahill-cycle and generates NAA instead of alanine as net product.
evidence: Based on biochemical calculations shown in Figure 8.

claim: NAA in the human brain is one of the most abundant metabolites and is routinely used in clinical MRI diagnosis to visualise brain health.
source: NAA in the human brain is one of the most abundant metabolites and is routinely used in clinical MRI diagnosis to visualise brain health (Igarashi et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on established knowledge with citation to Igarashi et al., 2015.

claim: NAA is a signature metabolite for the mini-Krebs-cycle.
source: While different functions have been hypothesised for NAA (Yan et al., 2003; Moffett et al., 2013), our work proposes NAA as a signature metabolite for the mini-Krebs-cycle.
evidence: Proposed based on metabolomics data with citations to Yan et al., 2003; Moffett et al., 2013.

claim: A recent study using Raman spectroscopy imaging detected high levels of NAA in the human retina, demonstrating in vivo use of the mini-Krebs-cycle.
source: Indeed, a recent study using Raman spectroscopy imaging detected high levels of NAA in the human retina, demonstrating in vivo use of this cycle (Alba-Arbalat et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alba-Arbalat et al., 2021.

claim: The 6-step mini-Krebs-cycle is significantly faster than the 10-step Krebs-cycle.
source: Importantly, the 6-step mini-Krebs-cycle is significantly faster than the 10-step Krebs-cycle (Yudkoff et al., 1994), more energy-efficient, and uncoupled from glycolysis.
evidence: Based on biochemical knowledge with citation to Yudkoff et al., 1994.

claim: The strong AST1/AST2 expression observed in the inner plexiform layer suggests that the mini-Krebs-cycle may also play a role in fuelling synaptic activity.
source: While the high metabolic rate of photoreceptors suggests that mini-Krebs-cycle metabolites will mostly originate there, the strong AST1/AST2 expression observed in the inner plexiform layer suggests that the mini-Krebs-cycle may also play a role in fuelling synaptic activity.
evidence: Inferred from enzyme expression data in Figure 7D.

claim: In rods, PCK1 may allow to replenish cytoplasmic acetyl-CoA pools from oxaloacetate, if BCAA-derived input was insufficient.
source: Moreover, in rods, PCK1 may allow to replenish cytoplasmic acetyl-CoA pools from oxaloacetate, if BCAA-derived input was insufficient.
evidence: Speculative inference from enzyme expression data in Figure 6B.

claim: The different pathways outlined provide photoreceptor cells with remarkable versatility and flexibility in terms of substrate use, enabling them to dynamically adapt the timing and quantitative output of energy metabolism.
source: Overall, the different pathways outlined here provide photoreceptor cells with remarkable versatility and flexibility in terms of substrate use, enabling them to dynamically adapt the timing and quantitative output of energy metabolism.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from all metabolomics and enzyme expression data.

claim: Rods rely strongly on the Krebs-cycle and OXPHOS, while cones are more dependent on glycolysis.
source: Rods rely strongly on the Krebs-cycle and OXPHOS, while cones are more dependent on glycolysis.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from differential treatment effects on rods and cones.

claim: The flexible uncoupling of glycolysis from mitochondrial respiration allows both processes to run at optimum, producing the characteristic signature metabolites lactate (Cori-cycle), alanine (Cahill-cycle), and NAA (mini-Krebs-cycle).
source: The flexible uncoupling of glycolysis from mitochondrial respiration allows both processes to run at optimum, producing the characteristic signature metabolites lactate (Cori-cycle), alanine (Cahill-cycle), and NAA (mini-Krebs-cycle).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from metabolomics data.

claim: These metabolites can reveal energy or disease status and could serve as readout and guide for the design of novel therapeutic interventions.
source: These metabolites can reveal energy or disease status and could serve as readout and guide for the design of novel therapeutic interventions.
evidence: Speculative conclusion about potential applications.

claim: The significance of the findings extends beyond the retina, for instance, to other neurodegenerative and metabolic diseases.
source: Given the general importance of energy metabolism, the significance of our findings extends beyond the retina, for instance, to other neurodegenerative and metabolic diseases.
evidence: Speculative conclusion about broader implications.
